result.what_is_wrong: Aggregate disparity metrics place race in the moderate-risk band: Disparate Impact = 0.9371 (below the 0.95 moderate threshold) and Demographic Parity Difference = -0.0512 indicate non-White groups receive favorable predictions at a lower rate than the privileged group (White). Error-rate metrics (Equal Opportunity Difference = 0.0032, Average Odds Difference = -0.0133) are near zero, so the model’s TPR/FPR tradeoffs are approximately balanced across groups, but that does not remove the observed selection-rate and base-rate gaps (e.g., White selection_rate 0.8128 vs Black 0.7447; Asian 0.8556; American Indian 0.6607; Multiracial 0.6383). The Theil index (0.296) further signals nontrivial inequality in the score/outcome distribution. Extreme sample-size imbalance (White n=6337 vs Pacific Islander n=27) creates large uncertainty for small groups and the potential for severe subgroup harms despite a moderate overall DI.
result.why_is_wrong: The most plausible mechanism is historical outcome bias plus proxying: prior discriminatory lending and structural socioeconomic differences produce different ground-truth base rates (labels) and feature distributions by race; the model can legitimately learn those correlations and reproduce disparate selection rates even when error rates look balanced. Features that correlate with race (neighborhood, income, credit history, application channel) act as proxies that encode structural bias into predictions. Very small groups (Pacific Islander, Multiracial, American Indian) have few records so their metrics have wide confidence intervals and high variance, meaning the audit both underestimates uncertainty and may miss severe harms to those subgroups. Thus the observed moderate DI reflects a real tendency for the model to perpetuate historical disparities and leaves subgroup-specific risks unresolved.
result.how_to_fix: Follow a staged remediation strategy combining targeted preprocessing, constrained training, and careful postprocessing plus data and evaluation steps: (1) Preprocessing: apply AIF360 Reweighing to compute race×label sample weights and retrain the model using those weights to reduce label-derived selection-rate bias; consider AIF360 DisparateImpactRemover if features themselves are strongly proxying for race and you prefer feature-level repair. (2) In-processing / constrained training: evaluate Fairlearn ExponentiatedGradient or GridSearch to optimize for a specified group-fairness constraint (e.g., demographic parity or bounded DI) while monitoring utility. (3) Postprocessing: if calibration/threshold control is required, apply AIF360 CalibratedEqOddsPostprocessing or Fairlearn ThresholdOptimizer to adjust decision thresholds per group; prefer CalibratedEqOddsPostprocessing when maintaining probabilistic calibration is important. (4) Small-group handling and evaluation: compute bootstrap confidence intervals for group metrics, consider pooling or targeted data collection for very small groups, and report uncertainty; avoid relying solely on point estimates for groups with n<30. (5) Governance: perform legal/regulatory review (fair-lending law), quantify fairness–utility tradeoffs, log and monitor post-deployment, and iterate. Measure the impact of each mitigation on DI, Demographic Parity Difference, EOD/AOD, Theil index, and subgroup confidence intervals before deployment.
